notes.front: On a cycle time chart, what does the 85th percentile line show?
notes.back: The Cycle Time within which 85% of past finished items were completed.
notes.explanation: Percentile lines (often 50th, 70th, 85th and 95th) turn past Cycle Times into a statement like “85% finish in 11 days or less”, which is the form an SLE takes.
notes.example: Sort your last 20 Cycle Times. If the 17th-fastest took 11 days, 85% finished in 11 days or less: the 85th percentile is 11 days.
notes.source: ProKanban.org blog, “Visualizing Flow Metrics: Where to Begin”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2026 ProKanban.org, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a cycle time scatterplot?
notes.back: A chart of each finished work item, plotted by when it finished and how long it took (its Cycle Time).
notes.explanation: With percentile lines on it, it shows the spread of past Cycle Times and is where an SLE is usually read from.
notes.example: Each dot is one finished item: a dot at x = 3 March, y = 6 means an item finished on 3 March after 6 days.
notes.source: ProKanban.org, The Kanban Playbook, question 4.2, “How far back should I look on my Cycle Time Scatterplot?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2026 ProKanban.org, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

Three horizontal lines: 50th percentile at 6 days (dotted), 70th percentile at 8 days (dashed) and 85th percentile at 11 days (solid), labelled “SLE: 85% of items finish in 11 days or less”. Three dots lie above the 11-day line, at 12, 14 and 18 days.

notes.front: What is an Aging WIP chart?
notes.back: A chart showing each item still in progress by its Work Item Age, set against the SLE or percentile lines.
notes.explanation: It is an in-flight signal: it shows which unfinished items are drifting past the expected delivery window while there is still time to act.
notes.example: A dot for item E, in Validating, at 13 days sits above the 11-day SLE line: it has already missed the SLE.
notes.source: ProKanban.org blog, “Visualizing Flow Metrics: Where to Begin”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2026 ProKanban.org, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

Discovery: A at 2 days, B at 7 days. Building: C at 4 days, D at 9 days. Validating: E at 13 days, F at 5 days. Horizontal lines mark the 50th (6 days), 70th (8 days) and 85th (11 days) percentiles of past Cycle Times.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from The Kanban Guide (Actively Managing Items in a Workflow) and The Kanban Pocket Guide, ch. 2 (facts only); data are illustrative

notes.front: What is arrival rate, in flow terms?
notes.back: How fast items arrive into a process, just as Throughput is how fast they depart.
notes.explanation: The Pocket Guide notes that how fast things arrive can matter as much as how fast they leave.
notes.example: If the Development step finishes 5 items a week, that is also the arrival rate into the next step, Test.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 6 “Throughput”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is a cumulative flow diagram (CFD)?
notes.back: A chart of the cumulative count of items arriving and departing over time, with bands for the workflow states.
notes.explanation: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams says a CFD can visualize WIP, approximate average Cycle Time and average Throughput.
notes.example: John Little, whose law comes a few cards on, used such a diagram, which he called a “Cumulative Arrivals/Departures diagram”, in a proof of his law.
notes.source: ProKanban.org blog, “Cumulative Flow Diagrams: Cutting Through the Colourful Clutter”; The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (Scrum.org, January 2021), “Sprint Retrospective”, p. 8; The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 1, PDF p. 21
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2026 ProKanban.org, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words (blog); B · CC BY-SA 4.0 (KGST); C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words (Pocket Guide)

notes.front: What does a throughput run chart show?
notes.back: Throughput for each day or week in turn, over time.
notes.explanation: It shows how consistently work is being finished, including periods when nothing finished.
notes.example: ProKanban's online lab plots items finished per week for a 46-item sample over 10 weeks.
notes.source: ProKanban.org, “The Kanban Pocket Guide” page, FAQ; ProKanban.org, The Kanban Playbook, question 4.1, “What flow metrics do I need, and when do I start?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2026 ProKanban.org, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is Little's Law, in the form the Kanban community uses?
notes.back: Average Cycle Time = Average WIP ÷ Average Throughput.
notes.explanation: It links three of the four flow metrics: in general, the more you work on at once (on average), the longer each item takes (on average).
notes.example: With an average WIP of 20 items and an average Throughput of 4 items a day, average Cycle Time is 5 days.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “An Introduction to Little's Law”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

image.alt: Diagram of Little's Law in its throughput form: Average Cycle Time equals Average WIP divided by Average Throughput. Below, its five assumptions in three groups. Conservation of Flow: 1, average arrival rate equals average throughput; 2, all started work finishes and leaves the system. System stability: 3, WIP about the same at the start and end of the period; 4, average age of WIP neither rising nor falling. Units: 5, Cycle Time, WIP and Throughput measured in consistent units. Footer: looks backward only, not a tool for deterministic forecasts.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from The Kanban Pocket Guide, Appendix A (facts only, in our own words)

notes.front: What is Conservation of Flow, in the Pocket Guide's account of Little's Law?
notes.back: The name for its first two assumptions: arrivals equal departures on average, and all started work finishes and leaves the system.
notes.explanation: Break these and the process becomes less predictable, and your data may look better than reality.
notes.example: A team that starts 10 items a week but finishes 6 is breaking Conservation of Flow.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “It is all about the Assumptions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is system stability, in the Pocket Guide's account of Little's Law?
notes.back: The name for its third and fourth assumptions: WIP about the same at the start and end of the period, and average WIP age steady.
notes.explanation: The Pocket Guide says every violation of an assumption makes the process less predictable.
notes.example: A board holding 12 items in January and 30 in March is not stable in this sense.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “It is all about the Assumptions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the Pocket Guide suggest using, instead of Little's Law, to make forecasts?
notes.back: Monte Carlo simulation on historical data, once the process mostly conforms to Little's Law's assumptions.
notes.explanation: Only then can the team trust its data enough to have confidence in the forecasts. Monte Carlo simulation is a method based on repeated random sampling; here it samples the team's own historical data many times.
notes.example: ProKanban's online lab runs 2,000 simulations on a team's data on demand.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “Forecasting”; Wikipedia, “Monte Carlo method” (lead section)
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words (Pocket Guide); B · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia)

notes.front: Does the Kanban Guide itself state Little's Law?
notes.back: No. It names queuing theory among Kanban's foundations, but Little's Law appears in other sources, such as the Pocket Guide.
notes.explanation: Learn it as background: it explains why controlling WIP matters.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Kanban Theory”, p. 4
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0

notes.front: How did John Little originally state his law?
notes.back: L = λW: average number of items in the system equals average arrival rate times average time in the system.
notes.explanation: The Cycle Time = WIP ÷ Throughput form came later from Operations Management, and needs different assumptions.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “We Need a Little Help”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Little's Law assumption 1: the average arrival rate should equal the average {{c1::Throughput}}.
notes.explanation: Work should start at about the same rate as it finishes.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “It is all about the Assumptions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Little's Law assumption 2: all work that is started eventually {{c1::finishes and leaves the system}}.
notes.explanation: Abandoned work breaks this assumption.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “It is all about the Assumptions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Little's Law assumption 3: WIP should be roughly the same at the {{c1::beginning and end}} of the period measured.
notes.explanation: The law says nothing about how much WIP is right, only that it should be stable.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “It is all about the Assumptions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Little's Law assumption 4: the average {{c1::age}} of the WIP is neither increasing nor decreasing.
notes.explanation: The Pocket Guide calls this the most important of the five for Kanban, because it is about items ageing unnecessarily.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “It is all about the Assumptions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Little's Law assumption 5: Cycle Time, WIP and Throughput must be measured in {{c1::consistent units}}.
notes.explanation: If Cycle Time is in days, Throughput must be items per day and WIP the average per day.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “It is all about the Assumptions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which of Little's Law's five assumptions are Conservation of Flow, and which are system stability?
notes.back: Assumptions 1 and 2 are Conservation of Flow; 3 and 4 are system stability.
notes.explanation: Assumption 5, consistent units, is needed for the arithmetic to come out right.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “It is all about the Assumptions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which Little's Law assumption does the Pocket Guide call the most important for Kanban?
notes.back: Assumption 4: the average age of WIP is neither increasing nor decreasing.
notes.explanation: Letting items age arbitrarily is, it says, the biggest reason teams are not effective, efficient or predictable.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 1 “The Most Important Part of Kanban: Work Item Age”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Can Little's Law be used to make deterministic forecasts?
notes.back: No. It only looks backward over a completed period; it is not meant for deterministic predictions.
notes.explanation: Forecasts from averages are also unreliable; Monte Carlo simulation on historical data is the suggested alternative.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “Forecasting”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Of Little's Law's three variables, which can a team control directly in real time?
notes.back: WIP.
notes.explanation: Cycle Time and Throughput respond to WIP and to how the system behaves; WIP is the lever.
notes.source: ProKanban.org, The Kanban Playbook, question 2.5, “Why should we control WIP?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2026 ProKanban.org, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: If Cycle Times are too long, what does Little's Law suggest a team consider first?
notes.back: Lowering WIP.
notes.explanation: Starting more work to “catch up” does the opposite: it makes items take longer.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (Scrum.org, January 2021), “Little's Law – The Key to Governing Flow”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0

notes.front: Does Little's Law require all work items to be the same size?
notes.back: No. It deals with averages, and item-size variation is usually not what hurts predictability most.
notes.explanation: Too much WIP and broken assumptions are usually bigger problems; where size matters, right-size rather than same-size.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “Size Does Not Matter”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When does the Pocket Guide say a team can start forecasting with Monte Carlo simulation?
notes.back: Once its process conforms, or mostly conforms, to Little's Law's assumptions, so its historical data can be trusted.
notes.explanation: The data from an unstable process gives an overly rosy or misleading picture.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “Forecasting”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Is an SLE a target the team must hit?
notes.back: No. It is a forecast of how long an item should take, based on data; ProKanban says it isn't a target.
notes.explanation: The Guide itself defines the SLE as a forecast of how long it should take a work item to flow from started to finished.
notes.source: ProKanban.org, “The Kanban Pocket Guide” page, FAQ
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2026 ProKanban.org, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: With an 85th-percentile SLE, what chance does an item have of missing it when it is first pulled in?
notes.explanation: That is what using the 85th percentile means: about 15 in 100 items take longer.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 2 “Percentiles as Intervention Triggers”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: With an 85th-percentile SLE, what is an item's chance of missing it once its age reaches the 50th percentile line?
notes.back: 30%: double the 15% it started with.
notes.explanation: It is now older than half the items seen before, which should at least prompt a conversation: swarm, split it, or escalate a blocker?
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 2 “Percentiles as Intervention Triggers”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: With an 85th-percentile SLE, what is an item's chance of missing it once its age reaches the 70th percentile line?
notes.back: 50%: a coin flip.
notes.explanation: The older an item gets, the more likely it is to get older, so action becomes more urgent.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 2 “Percentiles as Intervention Triggers”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Should a team start with one SLE for all its work, or one per type of work?
notes.back: One SLE for all work. ProKanban calls multiple SLEs a last resort, not a sign of maturity.
notes.explanation: Separate SLEs can hide flow problems such as too much WIP or unresolved blockers instead of fixing them.
notes.source: ProKanban.org, The Kanban Playbook, question 3.4, “Should I use multiple SLEs?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2026 ProKanban.org, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: If a team does use multiple SLEs, how much data should back each one, per ProKanban's playbook?
notes.back: At least 10 to 20 completed items of that type, each group showing stable flow.
notes.explanation: With fewer items, percentile lines shift from week to week.
notes.source: ProKanban.org, The Kanban Playbook, question 3.4, “Should I use multiple SLEs?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2026 ProKanban.org, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does ProKanban's playbook say classes of service tend to do to predictability?
notes.back: Add policy complexity and tend to hurt overall predictability rather than help it.
notes.explanation: Classes of service come from the Kanban Method, not the Kanban Guide.
notes.source: ProKanban.org, The Kanban Playbook, question 3.4, “Should I use multiple SLEs?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2026 ProKanban.org, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How far back should a cycle time scatterplot look?
notes.back: Only as far as the data still reflects how the current system works; there is no fixed number of weeks.
notes.explanation: Data from before a major workflow change distorts the percentile lines and so the SLE.
notes.source: ProKanban.org, The Kanban Playbook, question 4.2, “How far back should I look on my Cycle Time Scatterplot?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2026 ProKanban.org, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When reviewing an Aging WIP chart, which item does ProKanban suggest discussing first?
notes.back: The oldest item, asking what is stopping it from moving today.
notes.explanation: The chart is a daily signal; the oldest items are most at risk of missing the SLE.
notes.source: ProKanban.org blog, “Visualizing Flow Metrics: Where to Begin”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2026 ProKanban.org, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Does Little's Law describe individual items or averages?
notes.back: Averages: it is a relationship of averages.
notes.explanation: Averages are fine; problems start when people use the law for things it was never meant for, such as forecasts.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “We Need a Little Help”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which three things can a cumulative flow diagram visualize, per the Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams?
notes.back: WIP, approximate average Cycle Time and average Throughput.
notes.explanation: It suggests using a CFD in the Sprint Retrospective (the Scrum meeting that ends each Sprint) to inspect flow.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams (Scrum.org, January 2021), “Sprint Retrospective”; The Scrum Guide (November 2020), “Sprint Retrospective”
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0

notes.front: Of the metrics a CFD shows, which is an exact count rather than an average?
notes.back: WIP, at a given time.
notes.explanation: Cycle Time on a CFD is only approximate, and Throughput is an average over the chosen period.
notes.source: ProKanban.org blog, “Cumulative Flow Diagrams: Cutting Through the Colourful Clutter”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2026 ProKanban.org, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: When recording daily Throughput, what does ProKanban's playbook say to include?
notes.back: Zero-completion days, when nothing finished.
notes.explanation: Otherwise the record would skip the days when nothing finished, making Throughput look higher and steadier.
notes.source: ProKanban.org, The Kanban Playbook, question 4.1, “What flow metrics do I need, and when do I start?”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2026 ProKanban.org, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: From this illustrative cycle time scatterplot, what SLE would the team state at the 85th percentile?
notes.back: 85% of items finish in 11 days or less.
notes.explanation: An SLE has two parts: an elapsed time (11 days) and a probability (85%), read here from the 85th percentile line.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0

notes.front: Which of these illustrative CFDs suggests a stable system, and what does the other one show?
notes.back: A: arrivals and departures run roughly parallel. B's lines diverge, so WIP, and probably Cycle Time, are growing.
notes.explanation: ProKanban describes diverging lines as a crocodile opening its mouth: a red flag for stability.
notes.source: ProKanban.org blog, “Cumulative Flow Diagrams: Cutting Through the Colourful Clutter”

notes.front: Over the last month a team averaged 20 items in progress and a Throughput of 4 items per day. What was its average Cycle Time?
notes.explanation: Little's Law: average Cycle Time = average WIP ÷ average Throughput, in consistent units (items, days).
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “Forecasting”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A wine rack holds 100 bottles on average and is restocked at 2 bottles a week. On average, how long does a bottle stay in the rack?
notes.explanation: This is Little's own example of L = λW: knowing any two of the averages gives you the third.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “We Need a Little Help”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team plugs its velocity in story points per sprint into Little's Law as Throughput, with WIP counted in stories. What goes wrong?
notes.back: The units are inconsistent, breaking assumption 5, so the Cycle Time it calculates is meaningless.
notes.explanation: Throughput must be counted in items per the same unit of time used for Cycle Time and WIP.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “It is all about the Assumptions”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team averaged WIP 20, Cycle Time 5 days and Throughput 4 a day. A manager says doubling WIP to 40 will double Throughput to 8. Is that valid?
notes.back: No. Little's Law only says Cycle Time, Throughput or both will change; it cannot predict how.
notes.explanation: The law describes a completed period looking back; it is not a deterministic forecasting tool.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “Forecasting”
notes.sourceLicence: C · © 2022 Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A team often drops half-finished items when priorities change. Which Little's Law assumption does this break, and which group is it in?
notes.back: Assumption 2, that all started work finishes and leaves the system: part of Conservation of Flow.
notes.explanation: Abandoning work breaks Conservation of Flow and makes the process less predictable.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “It is all about the Assumptions”

notes.front: A team's bugs finish quickly but its features take weeks. With 6 finished bugs and 8 finished features, it sets separate SLEs for each. What would ProKanban's playbook advise?
notes.back: Start with one SLE and fix why features age; each separate SLE needs at least 10 to 20 completed items.
notes.explanation: With so little data the percentile lines shift weekly, and a separate SLE can make slow features feel acceptable.
notes.source: ProKanban.org, The Kanban Playbook, question 3.4, “Should I use multiple SLEs?”

notes.front: A team cut its WIP four months ago but its scatterplot still shows 12 months of data. What should it do?
notes.back: Filter the scatterplot to data from after the change, then update the SLE from the new percentile lines.
notes.explanation: Old data describes a system that no longer exists and makes the SLE wrong.
notes.source: ProKanban.org, The Kanban Playbook, question 4.2, “How far back should I look on my Cycle Time Scatterplot?”

notes.front: What is the difference between an SLE and a delivery target?
notes.back: An SLE is a data-based forecast (time plus probability); a target is a goal someone sets. The Guide defines the SLE as a forecast.
notes.explanation: An SLE should describe what is true of the system now.
notes.contrast: Describes the system versus demands of it.
notes.source: ProKanban.org, “The Kanban Pocket Guide” page, FAQ

notes.front: Which chart shows past performance, and which shows work in flight: the cycle time scatterplot or the Aging WIP chart?
notes.back: The scatterplot shows past performance (finished items); the Aging WIP chart shows work in flight (unfinished items).
notes.explanation: ProKanban suggests pairing them to look both back and ahead.
notes.source: ProKanban.org blog, “Visualizing Flow Metrics: Where to Begin”

notes.front: Once an item has breached its SLE, should the team ease off it?
notes.back: No. It still needs to be finished; a customer is still waiting for its value.
notes.explanation: The aim before the breach is to do everything possible to prevent it; after it, the work still matters.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 2 “Percentiles as Intervention Triggers”

notes.front: Should a CFD be used for forecasting?
notes.back: No. Its metrics are averages, so forecasts from it would be close to useless; use it to spot patterns and check stability.
notes.explanation: Forecasts built on averages hide the spread of real outcomes.
notes.source: ProKanban.org blog, “Cumulative Flow Diagrams: Cutting Through the Colourful Clutter”

notes.front: On this illustrative Aging WIP chart, Item B (7 days) has passed the 50th percentile line. What does that suggest?
notes.back: Its chance of missing the SLE has roughly doubled to 30%: time to talk about swarming, splitting it or clearing a blocker.
notes.explanation: Percentile lines work as checkpoints to act on an item before it misses the SLE.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 2 “Percentiles as Intervention Triggers”

notes.front: A board held 12 items at the start of the quarter and 30 at the end. Which group of Little's Law assumptions is broken?
notes.back: System stability: WIP should be roughly the same at the start and end of the period.
notes.explanation: It may also mean assumption 4 is broken; check the average age of WIP.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “It is all about the Assumptions”

notes.front: A team's Cycle Times keep rising, and a manager wants to start more items so they finish sooner. What does Little's Law suggest instead?
notes.back: Lower WIP: starting more work tends to make each item take longer, on average.
notes.explanation: WIP is the variable the team controls directly in real time.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “Little's Law from a Different Perspective”

notes.front: What is the difference between Little's Law and Monte Carlo simulation, as the Pocket Guide uses them?
notes.back: Little's Law checks, looking back, whether averages obey their relationship; Monte Carlo simulation forecasts from historical data.
notes.explanation: Meeting Little's Law's assumptions is what makes the data trustworthy enough for Monte Carlo forecasts.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), Appendix A, “Forecasting”
